subject: Discovery recap: Finly latency & streaming requirements
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Johnson <ajohnson@finly.com>
Cc: Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwood.ai>
Date: Fri, 13 Mar 2026 15:12:00 +0000
Subject: Discovery recap: Finly latency & streaming requirements

Alex — thanks again for the time today. Quick recap from our discovery so we have a shared baseline and clear next steps. Please flag anything I missed.

High-level pain points you described
- p95 latency currently ~800ms–1.6s for generation calls; worst-case spikes during peak trading windows.
- Streaming UX shows intermittent stalls (tokens arrive in bursts, making your traders perceive lag).
- Concurrency pressure: 150–300 concurrent streaming sessions at peak; need predictable tail latency under burst.
- Cost & predictability: current spend on hosted gen endpoints is rising with usage and multiple models.

Current stack (what you told us)
- Frontend: internal React UI with WebSocket streaming.
- Backend: FastAPI-based aggregator calling a third-party LLM endpoint (Open model via managed API).
- Minimal caching layer (short prefix cache) and no dedicated serving infra.

Success criteria for a POC
- p95 generation latency <= 350–400ms for typical prompts (~512 tokens max).
- Streaming token flush latency: visible incremental tokens within ~150–200ms intervals (improves UX).
- Support 200 sustained concurrent streaming sessions without p95 regression.
- End-to-end integration with your auth and logging; measurable cost per 1k tokens reporting.

Proposed next steps
1) Share representative prompt set and payload size distribution (tokens in/out).
2) Provide a short window of production traffic (redacted) or synthetic profiles so we can run a baseline load.
3) Team: Rishi (SE) will join the POC to run benchmarks and tuning.
4) Propose a 2-week POC: baseline run -> tuning (batching/kv-cache/quantization suggestions) -> final report and recommendations.

I attached a draft POC plan and the latency screenshot you shared in the call. I’ll follow up with available time slots for the baseline test next week.

Thanks,
Marissa Cole
Enterprise Sales
Redwood Inference

From: Alex Johnson <ajohnson@finly.com>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
Cc: Finly Procurement <procurement@finly.com>
Date: Fri, 13 Mar 2026 18:05:00 +0000
Subject: Re: Discovery recap: Finly latency & streaming requirements

Thanks Marissa — this is accurate, appreciate the clear write-up. Couple clarifications and additional detail from our side:

Details/clarifications
- Our p95 numbers are measured from the time the request leaves our edge -> response complete. We commonly see ~800ms median, p95 ~1.2s on average, and rare spikes to ~1.6s under load.
- Typical prompt distribution: 60% small prompts (~50–150 tokens), 30% medium (150–512), 10% long (>512 up to ~1k). Most streaming responses are in the medium bucket.
- Concurrency: our “peak” is about 220 concurrent streaming sessions for the market-content feature; we need room to scale to 300 for seasonal events.
- UX issue: frontend reports that the WebSocket stream often sends 2–3 token batches together instead of smooth 1–2 token increments; traders notice the burstiness.

What we can share
- I’ve attached a redacted 48-hour trace and our current latency dashboards as the zip. Procurement looped in for any contract/PO items.

POC success target (Finly)
- p95 <= 350ms for medium prompts (150–512 tokens) under 200 concurrent sessions.
- Streaming flush cadence <= 200ms so the UI feels near real-time.
- Cost: substantively better cost/throughput vs our current hosted provider for comparable tail latency.

We’re open to the 2-week POC. For scheduling, the week of Mar 22 works for our infra team.

–Alex
Alex Johnson
Head of Product (Market Content)
Finly

From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>

Cc: Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.ai>, Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwood.ai>, Finly Procurement <procurement@finly.com>
Date: Mon, 15 Mar 2026 09:30:00 +0000
Subject: Re: Discovery recap: Finly latency & streaming requirements

Great — thanks for the extra detail, Alex. Confirming next steps and a proposed schedule:

Action items from Redwood
- Rishi will prepare a benchmark harness (RWF-bench) that simulates your prompt distribution and streaming behavior.
- We’ll provision a staging Dedicated instance with a model suited to streaming (low-latency variant) and enable KV prefix caching + continuous batching.
- We’ll run a baseline load test (same payloads you sent) and capture p50/p95/p99 and streaming flush latencies.
- Post-baseline: tuning pass (adjust batching window, cache policies, and chunk sizes) and a second run. Deliverable: a short report with configuration recommendations and estimated unit cost.

Proposed timeline
- Week of Mar 22: baseline run (we’d need a 2-hour test window and an internal contact).
- Mar 24–26: tuning + follow-up run.
- Mar 29: delivery of results and recommended config.

What we need from Finly
1) Representative prompt set and a small script or endpoint we can hit (auth token) for synthetic traffic.
2) Clarify whether your WebSocket stream expects tokenized chunks every N ms or after a fixed token count. We can adjust flush intervals but need the exact client behavior.
3) Point contact during the 2-hour baseline (IAM token or temp staging route).

Compliance/contract notes
- Procurement — I’ll share a short SOW + standard POC terms (no production traffic, data retention controls). If you prefer a quick MSA/PO, we can parallelize contracting with the POC.

Does Mar 23 at 14:00 UTC for a short planning call work for your infra lead? If yes, I’ll send calendar invites and a DocuSign for the POC SOW.

From: Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Johnson <ajohnson@finly.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
Cc: Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 15 Mar 2026 14:07:00 +0000
Subject: Re: Discovery recap: Finly latency & streaming requirements

Quick note from the SE side — I’ll lead the benchmarking and tuning for the POC. A few technical asks so we can scope the harness appropriately:

1) Prompt templates and token distribution (you indicated — please drop as JSON or newline-delimited samples).
2) Typical max response length for streaming (tokens out) vs. average.
3) Concurrency profile: steady-state concurrency vs. short spikes (e.g., 220 steady vs. 300 spikes for 5–10 minutes).

Preliminary recommendations based on what we heard today
- Streaming UX: aim to flush token deltas <= 150ms if possible. We’ll experiment with 100–200ms.
- Batching/windowing: very small batching windows for streaming endpoints (10–20ms) with adaptive batching to avoid excessive latency on the p95 path.
- Caching: prefix KV cache for repeated prompts (market header/context) — this often brings p95 down significantly for conversational-ish calls.
- If model size allows, we’ll test int8 quantized variants to improve throughput/cost while watching tail latency.

I’ll draft the benchmark matrix and post it to the Drive link; Marissa — happy to lead the call on Mar 23 14:00 UTC if that works.

-Rishi
